pos: adj. and v. (starved; brought to the end of provision, in body or in soul)
etymology: From Latin fames, hunger, through Old French afamer. The Hebrew at Isaiah 5:13 is raab, the ordinary word for hunger and famine, and it is applied there to men of honour.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version uses this word, and the two places are a nation fed and a nation starved. In Egypt: “And when all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread: and Pharaoh said unto all the Egyptians, Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do” (Gen 41:55). The famine was foretold, the storehouses were filled during the years of plenty by a man his brethren had sold, and when the hunger came there was a place to be sent. In Judah the famine is of another kind: “Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge: and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst” (Isa 5:13). The cause is stated first — they have no knowledge — and the famishing of the honourable men follows it. Amos names this hunger directly: “I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11). A people may be well fed and famished; rank is no protection, for it is the honourable men Isaiah names.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to famish as to starve, to kill or destroy with hunger; and in the passive, to die or suffer extremity from want of food; also to exhaust the strength by hunger or thirst.
webster_full: FAMISH, v.t. [L. fames, hunger.] To starve; to kill or destroy with hunger.
2. To exhaust the strength of, by hunger or thirst; to distress with hunger.
FAMISH, v.i. To die of hunger; to starve; to suffer extreme hunger or thirst.
Their honourable men are famished. Isa. v.
scriptures: And when all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread: and Pharaoh said unto all the Egyptians, Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do.
Isa 5:13
Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge: and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst.
Amo 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
corruption_summary: A famine of hearing the words of the LORD is invisible to the people under it, which is why Isaiah 5:13 names the honourable men as the ones starving.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos describes the only famine a nation can suffer without noticing. Bread is missed at once; the absence of preaching is not, because a congregation which has not heard the word for years does not know what it has stopped receiving. The judgment falls in the form of abundance — more religious talk than ever, more books, more meetings, more music — while the actual exposition of Scripture is scarce. Isaiah supplies the diagnosis and puts it first in his sentence: because they have no knowledge. Not because they had no interest in religion; Judah was full of religion, and the earlier chapters are full of complaint about it. The famine is of knowledge, and it produces captivity.

The verse then adds the detail that makes it uncomfortable: their honourable men are famished. It is the men of standing who starve first, because they can furnish everything else and therefore feel no want. A man of means can commission whatever teaching flatters him; a man of position can be surrounded by agreement to the end of his life. Genesis 41 sets the mercy over against this. When the land was famished, Pharaoh had one thing to say — go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do — and the man he pointed to was the one his own people had put in a dungeon. God's ordinary way in a famine is to have prepared a granary beforehand and a despised man to keep it, and the only instruction the hungry are given is to go to him and do what he says.
roots_summary: Hebrew raab (H7456), to be hungry, to famish; tsameh (H6771), thirsty, in the parallel clause; both governed by the absence of daath (H1847), knowledge.
roots_lines: Hebrew raab (H7456) — to be hungry, to suffer famine; the honourable men are famished; Isaiah 5:13.
Hebrew daath (H1847) — knowledge; its absence is given as the cause of the captivity and the hunger; Isaiah 5:13, Hosea 4:6.
Hebrew raab as noun (H7458) — famine; the seven years foretold to Pharaoh and stored against; Genesis 41:30.
Hebrew tsammah — parched, dried up with thirst; the multitude of Isaiah 5:13.
Greek limos (G3042) — famine; the want in the far country that brought the prodigal to himself; Luke 15:14.
usage: “When all the land of Egypt was famished” — and a granary had been prepared beforehand.
“Their honourable men are famished” — rank starves first, because it can furnish everything else.
“A famine… of hearing the words of the LORD” — the one famine a people can suffer unaware.

pos: v. (made feeble; used chiefly of hands weakened in a work of God)
etymology: From Old English wac, pliant, weak. The Hebrew idiom in Ezra and Nehemiah is literally to let the hands drop — discouragement pictured as a tool falling out of a builder's grip.
biblical_def: The word attaches itself in Scripture to men who are building. Of the returned exiles: “Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building” (Ezr 4:4). Nehemiah records the same tactic and the answer to it in one verse: “For they all made us afraid, saying, Their hands shall be weakened from the work, that it be not done. Now therefore, O God, strengthen my hands” (Neh 6:9). The enemy's aim was never chiefly the wall; it was the hands. Fear was the instrument, and rumour, and letters, and invitations to talk in the plain of Ono — anything to make the builders let go. Nehemiah's prayer is six words long and asks for the exact thing being taken from him. The third use turns inward, where the weakening is God's own doing: “He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days” (Psa 102:23). The psalmist does not name an enemy at all; he names God. Both are true in Scripture — hands are weakened by opposition and by providence — and both drive to the same place: “He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength” (Isa 40:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to weaken as to make weak, to lessen the strength of, to debilitate, to enfeeble; and figuratively, to reduce in vigour, spirit or efficacy.
webster_full: WEAKEN, v.t. To lessen the strength of, or to deprive of strength; to debilitate; to enfeeble.
2. To reduce in vigor or spirit; to depress; as, to weaken the hands.
3. To reduce in force, efficacy or value.
The people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah. Ezra iv.
scriptures: Ezr 4:4
Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building,
Neh 6:9
For they all made us afraid, saying, Their hands shall be weakened from the work, that it be not done. Now therefore, O God, strengthen my hands.
He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days.
He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
corruption_summary: Discouragement is treated as a mood to be managed, when Ezra 4:4 presents it as a weapon deliberately used against a work of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The people of the land did not stop the building by force. They weakened hands — they hired counsellors, they wrote letters, they troubled the builders, and the work stood still for years. That is worth stating plainly because discouragement is usually treated as weather: a low season that comes over a man for no reason and must be waited out or medicated. Scripture treats it here as a campaign with authors and an objective, and Nehemiah names the objective in the enemy's own words — that it be not done. The application is not paranoia about opponents but a right assessment of what is happening when a man who was working finds his hands hanging down. Something is being attempted, and the counter is not chiefly analysis but prayer for the hands: strengthen my hands.

Psalm 102 keeps the doctrine honest against the opposite error, which is to blame every weakening on opposition or on the devil. The psalmist says he weakened my strength in the way — God did it, in the middle of the road, and shortened his days besides. There is a weakening that is providential, and it is not always chastisement for a fault; Paul's thorn was given him and not removed, and the answer he received put the whole matter on a different footing. The church that will not say with the psalmist that God weakened him is left with only two explanations for a servant laid low, and both are cruel: he must have sinned, or the enemy must have won. Scripture allows a third, and it ends where Isaiah 40 ends — strength given to those who have none, which is a different thing altogether from strength a man still has.
roots_summary: Hebrew raphah (H7503), to slacken, to let drop, used of the hands; anah (H6031), to afflict or humble, at Psalm 102:23; set against chazaq (H2388), to strengthen.
roots_lines: Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to sink, to let the hands drop; weakened the hands of the people of Judah; Ezra 4:4.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen; Nehemiah's prayer, strengthen my hands; Nehemiah 6:9.
Hebrew anah (H6031) — to afflict, to humble, to bring low; he weakened my strength in the way; Psalm 102:23.
Hebrew koach (H3581) — strength, power, ability; the thing weakened, and the thing God gives to the faint; Isaiah 40:29.
Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity; my strength is made perfect in weakness; 2 Corinthians 12:9.
usage: “Weakened the hands of the people of Judah” — discouragement as a campaign, not weather.
“Now therefore, O God, strengthen my hands” — six words asking for the thing being taken.
“He weakened my strength in the way” — and the psalmist names God, not an enemy.

pos: v. (diminished, lessened; used of floodwaters, of a valuation, of anger, and of a man's natural force)
etymology: Old French abatre, to beat down, from Latin ad and battere, to beat. The English keeps the sense of something brought down from a height — water, price, or wrath.
biblical_def: Four uses, and each one instructive. The flood: “Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground” (Gen 8:8) — and the reason they abated is given a few verses earlier: “God remembered Noah… and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged” (Gen 8:1). The law: a field sanctified after the jubile is reckoned by the years remaining, “and it shall be abated from thy estimation” (Lev 27:18) — the price falls because the time does, which is honest accounting written into the worship of God. Anger: Gideon turns away the wrath of Ephraim with a soft answer, and “their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that” (Jdg 8:3). And a man: “And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated” (Deu 34:7). That last is the exception that proves the rule, for natural force is exactly what does abate in every other man; Moses is buried by God with his strength unspent.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to abate as to beat down, to pull down, to destroy; to lessen, to diminish, to moderate; and in law, to deduct from a sum or a valuation.
webster_full: ABATE, v.t. [Fr. abattre, to beat down.] To beat down; to pull down; to destroy in any manner.
2. To lessen; to diminish; to moderate. Abate your speed.
3. To deduct; as, to abate a sum from an account.
ABATE, v.i. To decrease, or become less in strength or violence. The waters were abated. Gen. viii.
scriptures: Gen 8:8
Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground;
Gen 8:1
And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged;
Deu 34:7
And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated.

But if he sanctify his field after the jubile, then the priest shall reckon unto him the money according to the years that remain, even unto the year of the jubile, and it shall be abated from thy estimation.
corruption_summary: Floods are said to recede and tempers to cool as though by their own nature, while Genesis 8:1 assigns the abating to God remembering a man in a boat.
corruption_paragraphs: The waters did not simply drain away. Scripture puts a cause in front of the effect, and the cause is a Person: God remembered Noah, and made a wind to pass over the earth. That is the difference between the biblical account of the world and every account in which processes run themselves and God is at most the one who started them. A Christian may study evaporation and hydrology with the greatest diligence — the study is a good work and the regularity it describes is God's faithfulness — but he does not conclude from a mechanism that no one is governing it. Noah, for his part, is not idle either. He sends the dove, and sends her again, and waits seven days between; faith in the God who remembers is not the enemy of patient observation, it is what makes it bearable.

The Levitical use is the plainest place in Scripture where a valuation is honestly reduced. If a man sanctified his field after the jubile, the priest reckoned the years remaining and abated the estimate accordingly; the sanctuary did not take advantage of a worshipper's zeal to charge him for years that no longer existed. That is a small verse with a long reach, because religious institutions have a standing temptation to accept whatever a devout man will pay. And Deuteronomy 34:7 gives the other end of the word. Every man's natural force abates; the wonder recorded of Moses is that his did not, and the record is set down at the moment of his death, on the mountain, alone with God. He did not fail; he was taken. Which is the answer Scripture gives to men who dread the abating of their own strength: the strength is not the point of the life, and its keeping is not in the man.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaser (H2637), to lack or decrease, of the flood waters; garar and garaa (H1639), to diminish, of the abated estimation; raphah (H7503), to slacken, of anger.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaser (H2637) — to diminish, to be lacking; the waters were abated from off the face of the ground; Genesis 8:8.
Hebrew shakak (H7918) — to subside, to assuage; the waters asswaged when God made a wind to pass; Genesis 8:1.
Hebrew gara (H1639) — to diminish, to take away; abated from thy estimation; Leviticus 27:18.
Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to slacken; their anger was abated toward him; Judges 8:3.
Hebrew leach (H3893) — freshness, natural force; not abated in Moses at a hundred and twenty; Deuteronomy 34:7.
usage: “To see if the waters were abated” — and God had remembered Noah first.
“It shall be abated from thy estimation” — honest accounting written into the worship of God.
“Nor his natural force abated” — the exception, recorded at a grave God dug.

pos: v. (narrowed, confined, hemmed in; used of steps, of a building, of the Spirit, and of Christ's own soul)
etymology: From strait, narrow, Latin strictus, drawn tight — not the modern straight. To be straitened is to have the room taken away.
biblical_def: The picture is a narrowing. Of the wicked: “The steps of his strength shall be straitened, and his own counsel shall cast him down” (Job 18:7) — his stride shortens, and the thing that trips him is his own plan. Of the wise son, the exact reverse: “When thou goest, thy steps shall not be straitened; and when thou runnest, thou shalt not stumble” (Pro 4:12). Ezekiel uses it architecturally of a building narrowed in its upper storeys (Eze 42:6). Micah asks the question the presumptuous need: “is the spirit of the LORD straitened? are these his doings? do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly?” (Mic 2:7) — the false prophets had assumed God was confined to blessing them. Paul turns the word on a cold congregation: “Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels” (2Co 6:12) — the narrowness was in the Corinthians' affections, not in the apostle's. And most solemnly, the Lord Jesus uses it of Himself before the cross: “But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!” (Luk 12:50).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to straiten as to make narrow, to contract, to confine; to press with poverty or other necessity; to distress.
webster_full: STRAITEN, v.t. To make narrow.
2. To contract; to confine; as, to straiten a passage.
3. To make tense or tight; to extend.
4. To distress; to perplex; to press with poverty or other necessity. Thy steps shall not be straitened. Prov. iv.
scriptures: Job 18:7
The steps of his strength shall be straitened, and his own counsel shall cast him down.
Pro 4:12
When thou goest, thy steps shall not be straitened; and when thou runnest, thou shalt not stumble.
Mic 2:7
O thou that art named the house of Jacob, is the spirit of the LORD straitened? are these his doings? do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly?
But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!
corruption_summary: Micah 2:7 is quoted to prove that God is never limited, when the prophet asks it of men who had shrunk God to a guarantor of their own comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: The question is the spirit of the LORD straitened? is lifted out of Micah and made a slogan for expecting greater things, which is nearly the opposite of its use. The men addressed are the ones who told Jeremiah's and Micah's generation to prophesy smooth things — a house of Jacob confident that God's power was on call for their prosperity and could not be spoken against. Micah's reply has a second half that is always dropped: do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly? The promise is attached to a walk. God is not straitened; His good is not therefore owed to men who have taken the coat from off the garment and cast the women of His people out from their pleasant houses, which is what the same chapter charges them with. A doctrine of unlimited divine power detached from the character of the God who holds it is not faith, it is presumption with a proof text.

The apostolic use is more searching for a church. Paul had opened his mouth and enlarged his heart to the Corinthians, and told them plainly where the narrowness lay: ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels. Congregations become straitened in exactly this way. The affections narrow, the circle of those who are genuinely welcome contracts, and the fault is invariably located outside — in the preacher, in the newcomers, in the age. Paul's remedy is one imperative: be ye also enlarged. And over all of it stands the Lord's own use of the word, which forbids any sentimental reading. He was straitened until His baptism of blood was accomplished, pressed and confined by what lay before Him and pressing toward it. If the Son of God knew a narrowing of soul on the way to obedience, His servants need not conclude that constraint is a sign of God's displeasure.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsarar (H6887), to bind or be narrow; qatsar (H7114), to shorten; Greek stenochoreo (G4729), to be in a narrow place, and sunecho (G4912), to be held fast, at Luke 12:50.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsarar (H6887) — to be narrow, to bind, to distress; the steps of his strength shall be straitened; Job 18:7.
Hebrew qatsar (H7114) — to be short or shortened; is the spirit of the LORD straitened; Micah 2:7.
Greek stenochoreo (G4729) — to be in a narrow room, to be cramped; ye are straitened in your own bowels; 2 Corinthians 6:12.
Greek sunecho (G4912) — to hold together, to press, to constrain; how am I straitened till it be accomplished; Luke 12:50.
Greek splagchna (G4698) — the bowels, the seat of the affections in the biblical idiom; 2 Corinthians 6:12, Philippians 1:8.
usage: “His own counsel shall cast him down” — the narrowing that a man's own plan brings.
“Is the spirit of the LORD straitened?” — asked of men who had shrunk God to a guarantor.
“How am I straitened till it be accomplished!” — constraint of soul on the way to obedience.

pos: v. (dries up and fades; the standing biblical figure for the brevity of man)
etymology: From Middle English widren, akin to weather — to be dried by exposure. The Hebrew yabesh means simply to dry up, and it is what the east wind does to grass on a housetop.
biblical_def: This is the Bible's great comparison for human life, and it is never used to produce despair. “In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth” (Psa 90:6) — Moses' psalm, which draws from it the prayer to number our days. Job's friend uses it of the hypocrite's hope: “Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb” (Job 8:12). The psalmist prays it upon the enemies of Zion: “Let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up” (Psa 129:6) — seed on a roof has no depth of earth and dies before harvest. Isaiah gives the sentence its final form, and the whole comfort of the Bible turns on the second half: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass” (Isa 40:7); “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). Peter quotes it and identifies the abiding word: “this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you” (1Pe 1:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to wither as to fade, to lose freshness, to dry, to shrivel; and figuratively, to waste, to pine away, to lose vigour.
webster_full: WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its native freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth. Isa. xl.
2. To waste; to pine away; as animal bodies.
WITHER, v.t. To cause to fade and become dry; to cause to shrink, wrinkle and decay for want of moisture.
scriptures: Psa 90:6
In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth.
Isa 40:7
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:
corruption_summary: Man's brevity is either denied by an industry that promises indefinite extension, or made a reason for despair; Isaiah puts it beside the abiding word and makes it a comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's clause gives a cause that is almost never quoted with the rest: the grass withereth because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it. Withering is not an accident of biology; it is the breath of God on a field. That single line rules out both of the errors men fall into here. It rules out the account in which death is simply what organisms do, a fact with no author and therefore no meaning, which is the working assumption of most public speech about mortality. And it rules out the pretence, sold at enormous expense, that the withering can be indefinitely postponed by regimen, surgery or technology. Moses drew the only sane conclusion in the same breath as the figure: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. A man who knows he is grass can plan honestly; a man who has been told he is a machine in need of maintenance cannot.

The other error runs among believers, and it is to leave the sentence unfinished. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth — quoted alone, at a graveside, it is a stone. Isaiah does not stop there and neither does Peter. The clause that follows is the whole hope: but the word of our God shall stand for ever, and Peter adds that this abiding word is the gospel preached to us. So the contrast is not between a short life and a long book. It is between flesh, which fades, and a word that both endures and, being received, makes the hearer a partaker of what endures — born again, Peter says, of incorruptible seed. Psalm 129's grass on the housetop makes the same point from the other side: what has no root does not last, whatever green it shows in the morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew yabesh (H3001), to dry up, to wither; with nabel (H5034), to fade or fall; Greek xeraino (G3583), to dry up, in Peter's quotation of Isaiah.
roots_lines: Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to be dry, to wither; the grass withereth; Isaiah 40:7, Psalm 90:6.
Hebrew nabel (H5034) — to fade, to fall away, to be foolish; the flower fadeth; Isaiah 40:7.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath, spirit; the spirit of the LORD that bloweth upon the grass; Isaiah 40:7.
Greek xeraino (G3583) — to dry up, to wither; the grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away; 1 Peter 1:24.
Greek rhema (G4487) — a spoken word; the word of the Lord that endureth for ever and is preached as the gospel; 1 Peter 1:25.
usage: “In the evening it is cut down, and withereth” — and Moses prays to number his days.
“Because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it” — withering with an Author.
“But the word of our God shall stand for ever” — the half of the verse that must not be dropped.

pos: v. (loosed apart, broken up; used of cities, of the earth, and of the host of heaven)
etymology: Latin dissolvere, to loosen apart, from dis-, asunder, and solvere, to loose. What is dissolved is not merely damaged; the bonds that held it together are undone.
biblical_def: Scripture reserves this word for the undoing of things men assume are permanent. A city: “Howl, O gate; cry, O city; thou, whole Palestina, art dissolved” (Isa 14:31). A palace: “The gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved” (Nah 2:6). The earth itself: “The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly” (Isa 24:19). Even the sky: “And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll” (Isa 34:4). Against this the psalmist hears God speak in the first person: “The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah” (Psa 75:3). The dissolution is real and the pillars are borne up by a hand; both clauses stand in one verse. Peter draws the practical conclusion and it is not speculation about dates but a question about character: “Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness” (2Pe 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to dissolve as to melt, to liquefy; to break, to disunite, to loosen the parts of a thing; and to break up an assembly or dissolve a body politic.
webster_full: DISSOLVE, v.t. dizzolv'. [L. dissolvo; dis and solvo, to loose.] To melt; to liquefy; to convert from a solid or fixed state to a fluid state.
2. To disunite; to break; to separate.
3. To loose; to disunite; as, to dissolve a league or a friendship.
All these things shall be dissolved. 2 Pet. iii.
scriptures: The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly.
Isa 34:4

And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree.
Psa 75:3
The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah.
Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness,
corruption_summary: The dissolution of all things is treated either as poetry that means nothing or as a calendar to be decoded, while Peter draws from it one plain question about how a man lives.
corruption_paragraphs: Two habits keep the church from hearing 2 Peter 3. The first empties the language: the passage is called apocalyptic imagery, a way of speaking about upheaval in general, and the plain assertion that the elements shall melt with fervent heat is quietly filed as a figure. The apostle's own argument forbids it — he grounds the coming dissolution in a past event of the same kind, the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished, and he says the scoffers of the last days will be men who are willingly ignorant of that flood. Deny the first judgment and the second becomes unimaginable, which is exactly the mechanism he describes. The second habit is the mirror image: the passage becomes a code, matched against current events, and a generation is fed dates that pass. Peter draws no date from it at all. From all these things shall be dissolved he draws one question, and it concerns conduct.

Psalm 75:3 keeps the doctrine from becoming terror. In one verse the earth and all its inhabitants are dissolved, and God says I bear up the pillars of it. Nothing dissolves outside His hand, and the same hand that will one day fold the heavens as a scroll is holding the floor up under the reader this morning. That is why the Christian doctrine of the last things is not a doctrine of panic, and why the practical counsel that flows from it is holy conversation and godliness rather than hoarding or withdrawal. A man who knows the house is coming down invests in what will not, and Peter says exactly what that is in the following verse: we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.
roots_summary: Hebrew mug (H4127), to melt or dissolve; parar (H6565), to break apart; Greek luo (G3089), to loose, used by Peter of the dissolving of all things.
roots_lines: Hebrew mug (H4127) — to melt, to dissolve; the earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved; Psalm 75:3.
Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, to make void; the earth is clean dissolved; Isaiah 24:19.
Hebrew maqaq (H4743) — to pine away, to melt; all the host of heaven shall be dissolved; Isaiah 34:4.
Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, to break up; all these things shall be dissolved; 2 Peter 3:11.
Greek stoicheion (G4747) — an element, a first principle; the elements that shall melt with fervent heat; 2 Peter 3:10.
usage: “The earth is clean dissolved” — the undoing of what men assume is permanent.
“I bear up the pillars of it” — in the same verse as the dissolving.
“What manner of persons ought ye to be” — the only inference Peter draws.

pos: v. and adj. (fallen away, wasted; used of a builder's strength and of ruined places God promises to raise)
etymology: Old French decair, from Latin de-, down, and cadere, to fall — a falling away by degrees rather than at a stroke.
biblical_def: The word appears at the hardest moment of Nehemiah's work and in the sweetest promise of Isaiah. On the wall: “And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall” (Neh 4:10). Three things are named — failing strength, too much rubble, and a conclusion drawn from them. It is the conclusion that is fatal, and it comes from within the workforce, not from Sanballat. Nehemiah's answer in the following verses is to set the people by families with a weapon in one hand, and the wall was finished in fifty and two days. Against this stands Isaiah's word about the God who reverses decay: “That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers; that saith to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah, Ye shall be built, and I will raise up the decayed places thereof” (Isa 44:26). And Paul says the same of the body a Christian is living in: “though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2Co 4:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines decay as a gradual failure of health, strength, soundness or prosperity; a falling into a worse state; and to decay as to pass from a state of soundness gradually to a worse.
webster_full: DECAY, v.i. [L. de and cado, to fall.] To pass gradually from a sound, prosperous, or perfect state, to a less perfect state, or towards weakness or dissolution.
2. To fail; to decline; to be gradually impaired.
DECAY, n. Gradual failure of health, strength, soundness, prosperity, or of any species of excellence or perfection.
The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed. Neh. iv.
scriptures: Neh 4:10
And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall.
Neh 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.

That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers; that saith to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah, Ye shall be built, and I will raise up the decayed places thereof:
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
corruption_summary: Nehemiah 4:10 is quoted as a description of burnout, when the verse's sting is not the tiredness but the sentence drawn from it — we are not able.
corruption_paragraphs: Everything Judah says in Nehemiah 4:10 is factually true. The bearers of burdens were exhausted; there was a great deal of rubbish; the wall was half built and the enemy was massing. Scripture does not rebuke the report, and it is a mistake to preach this verse as though weariness were sin — four verses earlier the same people had a mind to work, and the Lord Jesus Himself sat down at a well being wearied with His journey. The failure is in the last clause: so that we are not able to build the wall. A true account of the strength has been turned into a verdict about the outcome, and the verdict leaves God out. That is the point at which honest tiredness becomes unbelief, and it is a very short step, taken quietly, usually by the most diligent workers rather than the idle ones.

Nehemiah's response is worth marking because it is not a speech about attitude. He set the people by their families with swords, spears and bows; he arranged for the trumpet to gather them; he told them plainly, our God shall fight for us. Encouragement in Scripture is nearly always concrete — a reordering of the work, a weapon in the hand, a reminder of a specific promise — rather than an appeal to feel differently. And Isaiah 44:26 supplies the promise that answers decay at the root: God says to cities in ruins that they shall be built, and He is described in that same verse as the One who confirms the word of His servant. The decayed places are raised by the word of a God who keeps His word, which is precisely why a man may report his weakness honestly and still refuse the sentence we are not able.
roots_summary: Hebrew kashal (H3782), to stumble or totter, of the failing strength; chorbah (H2723), a waste or desolate place, the decayed places God promises to raise.
roots_lines: Hebrew kashal (H3782) — to stumble, to totter, to fail; the strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed; Nehemiah 4:10.
Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a ruin, a desolation; I will raise up the decayed places thereof; Isaiah 44:26.
Hebrew aphar (H6083) — dust, rubbish; the heaps out of which the wall was rebuilt; Nehemiah 4:2.
Hebrew qum (H6965) — to rise, to raise up, to confirm; God confirms the word of his servant and raises the ruins; Isaiah 44:26.
Greek diaphtheiro (G1311) — to corrupt utterly, to perish; though our outward man perish; 2 Corinthians 4:16.
usage: “The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed” — an honest report.
“So that we are not able to build the wall” — the sentence that leaves God out.
“I will raise up the decayed places thereof” — said by the God who confirms His servant's word.

pos: v. (poured out and lost; used of Onan's seed and of new wine in old bottles)
etymology: Old English spillan, to destroy or waste, later narrowed to the shedding of a liquid. The older sense of ruin is still audible in the Authorized Version's use.
biblical_def: Genesis records the sin that took Onan's life: “And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother” (Gen 38:9). The text is careful to give the motive — he knew the seed should not be his — so the sin is not merely an act but the calculated refusal of a duty owed to a dead brother's name under the levirate law, using the form of obedience while defeating its purpose. The Lord's parable uses the same word for a different loss: “And no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred” (Mar 2:22); Luke has it in nearly the same words (Luk 5:37). Here nothing is sinful, only unfit: old skins have lost their stretch, and new wine in ferment will split them, so that both the wine and the skins are lost. Set against both is the Lord's command over the fragments after feeding the five thousand: “Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost” (Joh 6:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives to spill as to suffer to fall or run out of a vessel; to shed; and in the older sense, to destroy, to waste, to bring to ruin.
webster_full: SPILL, v.t. To suffer to fall or run out of a vessel; to lose, or suffer to be scattered; applied only to fluids and to substances whose particles are small and loose.
2. To shed; to suffer to flow out; as, to spill blood.
3. To destroy; to ruin. [Obs. in this sense, but retained in Scripture.]
The new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled. Mark ii.
scriptures: Gen 38:9
And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother.
Mar 2:22
And no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred: but new wine must be put into new bottles.
Luk 5:37
And no man putteth new wine into old bottles; else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled, and the bottles shall perish.
Joh 6:12
When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost.
corruption_summary: The parable of the new wine is used to justify discarding whatever is old in the church, though the Lord's point is the unfitness of a worn vessel, not the worthlessness of what came before.
corruption_paragraphs: New wine and old bottles has become the standard proof text for novelty: the old forms must go, the new movement cannot be contained by them, and whoever objects is an old skin. The Lord's meaning in context is narrower and sharper. He is answering a question about fasting, and the old bottles are the Pharisaic system — a legal frame that could not hold the gospel of the kingdom — not the Old Testament, which He came to fulfil and not to destroy. Luke, who tells the same parable, adds a sentence the users of the slogan never quote: no man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new, for he saith, The old is better. The passage is not a licence to dispose of confessions, catechisms, forms of worship and the psalter because a movement feels fresh. What it warns against is trying to contain the living work of God inside a system built to keep men out.

Genesis 38 is the harder half. Onan is not condemned for a private act considered by itself but for the calculated defeat of a duty: he took the privilege of the marriage and withheld the purpose of it, so that his brother's name should not be raised up and the inheritance should fall to himself. That is what the text supplies as motive, and it is the reason the thing displeased the LORD. Two applications follow and both are unwelcome in our moment. Marriage in Scripture is not detachable from the raising of a name and a household; and a man who takes the pleasures of an estate while refusing its obligations is doing what Onan did, whatever the estate. Over against the waste stands the Lord at the end of the miracle, commanding the fragments to be gathered that nothing be lost — the God who feeds thousands from a boy's dinner is also the God who will not have the leftovers spilled.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath (H7843), to spoil or destroy, of Onan's act; Greek ekcheo (G1632), to pour out, of the wine; set against apollumi (G622), to lose or perish, in John 6:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to mar, to spoil, to destroy; he spilled it on the ground; Genesis 38:9.
Hebrew yabam (H2992) — to perform the duty of a husband's brother; the levirate obligation Onan defeated; Deuteronomy 25:5.
Greek ekcheo (G1632) — to pour out, to spill; the new wine spilled from burst skins; Mark 2:22.
Greek askos (G779) — a leathern bottle, a wineskin; the vessel that has lost its stretch; Luke 5:37.
Greek apollumi (G622) — to destroy, to lose; that nothing be lost, said over the fragments; John 6:12.
usage: “He spilled it on the ground” — the form of the duty kept, the purpose defeated.
“The new wine doth burst the bottles” — a worn vessel, not a worthless past.
“Gather up the fragments… that nothing be lost” — the Lord's own economy.

pos: v. (stopped, smothered; the word of the parable for a word that is prevented from bearing fruit)
etymology: Middle English choken, to stop the breath. The Greek sumpnigo is a compound — to press together and strangle — used of thorns around wheat and of a crowd pressing about Christ.
biblical_def: The word belongs to the parable of the sower, where it names the third soil and the most respectable failure. “And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them” (Mat 13:7); Mark adds the outcome, “and it yielded no fruit” (Mar 4:7). The Lord Himself supplies the interpretation, and it is remarkable for containing nothing scandalous: “And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection” (Luk 8:14). Matthew names two of the three: “the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful” (Mat 13:22). Not persecution, not heresy, not open sin — anxiety, money and pleasure, all three of them ordinary. The same verb is used of the swine at Gadara, which “ran violently down a steep place into the sea… and were choked in the sea” (Mar 5:13). Thorns do not attack the seed; they simply grow in the same ground, and take the light.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to choke as to stop the passage of the breath; to suffocate; and figuratively, to obstruct, to stop, to hinder or check the growth of anything.
webster_full: CHOKE, v.t. To stop the passage of the breath, by filling the windpipe or compressing the neck; to suffocate; to stifle.
2. To stop by filling; to obstruct; to block up; as, to choke a passage.
3. To hinder or check growth, expansion or progress. The thorns sprung up and choked them. Matt. xiii.
4. To smother or suffocate, as fire.
scriptures: Mat 13:7
And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them:
Luk 8:14
And that which fell among thorns are they, which, when they have heard, go forth, and are choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and bring no fruit to perfection.
He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful.
Mar 4:7
And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up, and choked it, and it yielded no fruit.
corruption_summary: The thorny ground is preached as a warning against gross sin, when the Lord names cares, riches and pleasures — three things a respectable congregation will not call sins at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in the Lord's own interpretation of the thorns is disreputable. Cares is anxiety about real matters — a mortgage, a diagnosis, a child. Riches is money, described as deceitful rather than as evil, because its lie is that it can secure what only God secures. Pleasures of this life are lawful enjoyments. Not one of the three would be named in a testimony as the thing that ruined a man, and that is precisely why the Lord names them. A hearer is not choked by an obvious rival; he is choked by a hundred legitimate things growing in the same soil until there is no room left. And the outcome is not apostasy with a bang but a slow unfruitfulness: he brings no fruit to perfection, which is to say the growth begins and is never completed.

It is worth being exact about what the parable does and does not prove. The thorny ground is not a picture of a true believer losing his salvation; the same Lord who spoke this parable said that of all the Father gave Him He should lose nothing. It is a picture of a hearing that never came to fruit, and Scripture's consistent mark of genuine life is fruit that appears and continues, however slowly. The pastoral use is therefore self-examination rather than the sorting of other men into soils. A Christian may ask, plainly, which of the three is growing in his ground this year, and act on the answer — for thorns are not removed by resolving to bear fruit but by being pulled up. Christ Himself wore a crown of them, which is the ground of any hope that the field can be cleared at all.
roots_summary: Greek sumpnigo (G4846), to press together and strangle; with merimna (G3308), care or anxiety, apate ploutou (G539, G4149), the deceitfulness of riches, and hedone (G2237), pleasure.
roots_lines: Greek sumpnigo (G4846) — to choke utterly, to press together; of the thorns and of the crowd thronging Christ; Luke 8:14, Luke 8:42.
Greek merimna (G3308) — care, anxiety, a divided mind; the first thorn; Matthew 13:22, 1 Peter 5:7.
Greek apate (G539) — deceit; joined to riches, which promise a security they cannot give; Matthew 13:22.
Greek hedone (G2237) — pleasure, gratification; the third thorn, and the root of the English hedonism; Luke 8:14, James 4:3.
Greek telesphoreo (G5052) — to bring to completion or perfection; what the choked hearer never does with fruit; Luke 8:14.
usage: “The thorns sprung up, and choked them” — no attack, only the same ground and the light taken.
“Choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life” — three things nobody confesses.
“Bring no fruit to perfection” — growth begun and never completed.

pos: v. (gave off a stench; used of judgment on Egypt, of hoarded manna, and of a nation's ruined name)
etymology: Old English stincan, to emit a smell of any kind, narrowed in English to an offensive one. The Hebrew baash means both to stink and to become odious — a reputation and a smell in one word.
biblical_def: Three uses, and each is a judgment. The first plague: “And the fish that was in the river died; and the river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink of the water of the river” (Exo 7:21). Then the frogs: “And they gathered them together upon heaps: and the land stank” (Exo 8:14) — the plague was over and the stench was worse than the plague, because Pharaoh had asked for a delay of one day before relief. Then the manna: “Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them” (Exo 16:20). Bread given daily and hoarded overnight rots; the same bread kept for the sabbath by God's own command did not. The fourth use carries the Hebrew's other sense, of a name made odious: “when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David” (2Sa 10:6), after they had shamed his ambassadors. In every case the stench is the visible end of something men thought they had managed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives stink as to emit a strong offensive smell, and stank as its past tense; figuratively, to be odious or offensive, as a name in disrepute.
webster_full: STINK, v.i. pret. stank or stunk. To emit a strong offensive smell.
2. To be in bad repute; to be odious. They stank before David. 2 Sam. x.
STINK, n. A strong offensive smell.
It bred worms, and stank. Ex. xvi.
scriptures: Exo 7:21
And the fish that was in the river died; and the river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink of the water of the river; and there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.
Exo 8:14
And they gathered them together upon heaps: and the land stank.
Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them.

And when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David, the children of Ammon sent and hired the Syrians of Bethrehob, and the Syrians of Zoba, twenty thousand footmen, and of king Maacah a thousand men, and of Ishtob twelve thousand men.
corruption_summary: Hoarded manna is the plainest picture in Scripture of trying to secure tomorrow out of today's provision, and it is generally read as a quaint story rather than as an economy.
corruption_paragraphs: The manna is not a lesson against saving; the same law that forbade keeping it overnight commanded a double portion gathered on the sixth day, and that portion did not rot. Scripture elsewhere praises the ant and the prudent man, and the seven years of plenty in Egypt were stored on God's own instruction. The sin at Exodus 16:20 is precise: they hearkened not unto Moses. God had said the bread would come every morning, and some of them arranged an insurance against His word. What they kept bred worms by dawn. The distinction the passage draws is between saving under God's direction and saving against God's promise, and it cannot be settled by the size of the store — it is settled by whether a man is obeying or hedging. The Lord's prayer keeps the same rhythm: give us this day our daily bread.

The frogs supply the other lesson, and it is about delay. Moses asked Pharaoh when he should entreat for the removal of the plague, and Pharaoh said, To morrow — one more night with the frogs rather than immediate relief, for reasons the text does not explain and does not need to. The frogs died, were gathered upon heaps, and the land stank. Sin left one more day does not stay the same size; it decays where it lies. That is worth saying plainly to a Christian who intends to deal with something and has decided that tomorrow will do. And the last use, the Ammonites who stank before David, shows a nation discovering that an insult it had enjoyed making was a stench it could not now wash off — so it hired thirty-three thousand men to defend what a word of apology would have settled.
roots_summary: Hebrew baash (H887), to stink and to become odious; used of the river, the land, the hoarded manna, and a nation's name.
roots_lines: Hebrew baash (H887) — to have a bad smell, and figuratively to be abhorred; the river stank, and Ammon stank before David; Exodus 7:21, 2 Samuel 10:6.
Hebrew man (H4478) — manna, the bread whose name means what is it; given daily and not to be kept; Exodus 16:15.
Hebrew rimmah (H7415) — a maggot, a worm; it bred worms, and stank; Exodus 16:20.
Hebrew machar (H4279) — to morrow; Pharaoh's answer when offered relief from the frogs; Exodus 8:10.
Greek ozo (G3605) — to smell, to give off odour; by this time he stinketh, said of Lazarus four days dead; John 11:39.
usage: “The river stank” — the first plague, at the water Egypt worshipped.
“It bred worms, and stank” — insurance taken out against a promise.
“They stank before David” — an insult that could not be washed off.
